entities.name: Tsitsernakaberd
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Tsitsernakaberd, the Armenian Genocide Memorial complex located in Yerevan, Armenia, stands as a solemn tribute to the estimated 1.5 million victims of the Armenian genocide perpetrated by the Ottoman Empire from 1915 to 1923. Designed by architects B. Z. Mkhitaryan and A. M. Kasyan, the memorial was inaugurated on April 24, 1967, a date that has since become synonymous with Armenian Genocide Remembrance Day. This site not only marks a pivotal moment in the history of Armenia but also serves as a crucial symbol in the global discourse on genocide and human rights, reflecting the broader struggle for recognition and justice faced by the Armenian people.

The memorial itself features a striking 44-meter tall stele representing the 44 days of the genocide, surrounded by twelve slabs symbolizing the twelve lost provinces of historic Armenia. Each year, on April 24, crowds gather to lay flowers, light candles, and hold memorial services in an act of collective mourning and remembrance. The complex also includes a museum that educates visitors about the genocide, aiming to prevent future atrocities through awareness and recognition. The memorial has become a focal point for Armenian diaspora communities worldwide, reinforcing their identity and commitment to the memory of their ancestors.

The legacy of Tsitsernakaberd extends beyond mere commemoration; it has catalyzed international recognition of the Armenian genocide, influencing legislative measures in various countries. The site has inspired similar memorials around the world, contributing to a global movement that seeks to acknowledge and learn from historical injustices. In a poignant reflection of its impact, the memorial reminds us that 'the first step towards healing is recognition,' a principle that resonates deeply within the ongoing struggles for justice faced by oppressed peoples globally.
